Persia
pûr'zhă
n. (the empire that succeeded Babylon — the power under which the temple was rebuilt, the wall raised, and a Jewish queen saved her people)
From Hebrew Paras, Persia; the same consonants as the word peres, divided, in the writing on Belshazzar's wall — a pun the reader is meant to hear.

Biblical Definition

Persia enters Scripture as an answer to prayer. Babylon had taken Judah captive; Persia sent Judah home. “Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” (Ezr 1:1) — and the seventy years ended precisely as foretold, by the decree of a pagan whom Isaiah had named a century and a half before he was born. Under Persian kings the second temple was built, Ezra brought the law, Nehemiah raised the wall, and Esther's deliverance was wrought in Shushan the palace. Daniel sees the empire as a ram with two horns — “the kings of Media and Persia” (Dan 8:20) — and its constitutional peculiarity becomes a plot device twice over: “the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8), which threw Daniel to the lions and which Haman's decree against the Jews could not undo, only counter. Persia is the empire under which the whole post-exilic Old Testament takes place. It is remembered not for cruelty but for a strange, ordered, unwitting service to the purposes of God — a reminder that the Lord governs by decrees He never asks a king to understand.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives Persia as a large country of Asia, and Persian as pertaining to it, noting the empire founded by Cyrus which succeeded that of Babylon.

expand to see more

PERSIA, n. A country of Asia, bounded by the Caspian on the north and the Persian gulf on the south.

The Persian empire was founded by Cyrus, who overthrew the Chaldean monarchy and took Babylon.

By his decree the Jews returned from captivity and the house of the Lord at Jerusalem was rebuilt.

The laws of the Medes and Persians were held unalterable, once signed by the king.

The empire was overthrown by Alexander of Macedon, as foreshown in the visions of Daniel.

Key Scripture

Ezr 1:1 — "Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying,"

2Ch 36:20 — "And them that had escaped from the sword carried he away to Babylon; where they were servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia:"

Dan 8:20 — "The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia."

Dan 6:8 — "Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not."

Modern Corruption

Daniel's naming of Persia and Greece in advance is the chief reason critics date the book to the second century; the argument assumes at the outset that prophecy cannot happen.

expand to see more

The four empires of Daniel are the pivot of the argument over the book's date. Because the visions describe the Persian and Greek periods with accuracy, the standard critical position places the writing after those events, in the days of Antiochus. Note the structure of the reasoning: predictive prophecy is excluded before the evidence is weighed, so accuracy becomes proof of lateness. The dictionary holds the sixth-century Daniel of the Hebrew canon — the man Ezekiel names among the righteous (Eze 14:14), whose book the Lord Jesus cites as spoken “by Daniel the prophet” (Mat 24:15). If God foretells, then a book that foretells is what it claims to be, and the internal Aramaic, the Persian loanwords, and the Babylonian court detail fit a writer who was there.

The second corruption is smaller but worth naming: the habit of reading Cyrus as a model of enlightened tolerance and stopping there. Ezr 1:1 does not say Cyrus was tolerant. It says the LORD stirred up his spirit so that Jeremiah's word might be fulfilled. Isa 45 goes further and calls him by name, “my shepherd” and even the LORD's anointed, and then says plainly, “I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me” (Isa 45:4). A ruler can be the instrument of a covenant purpose he has never heard of. That is a comfort in every generation, and it is not a reason to baptise the ruler.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Paras (H6539), Persia; Paras also puns on peres (H6537), divided, in Dan 5:28; 'ur (H5782), to stir up.

expand to see more

Hebrew Paras (H6539) — Persia, Persian; the empire of Cyrus, Darius, and Ahasuerus.

Aramaic peres (H6537) — divided; the third word on Belshazzar's wall, sounding the name of the conqueror.

Hebrew 'ur (H5782) — to rouse, stir up; what the LORD did to the spirit of Cyrus (Ezr 1:1).

Hebrew dath (H1881) — a decree, law; the Persian edict that could not be altered.

Hebrew Shushan (H7800) — Shushan, Susa, the palace-city of Esther and of Daniel's later visions.

Usage

"“The LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” — a pagan decree fulfilling a prophet's word."

"“The kings of Media and Persia” — the two-horned ram of Daniel's vision."

"“The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” — a constitution that trapped its own king."
